Tahini in particular has been linked to Salmonella outbreaks and recalls. The hazard analysis does not cover this. / Add hazard analysis rows for pathogens in each ingredient added after cooking. Then name the control for each one: a supply-chain-applied control with supplier verification, a validated process step on the supplier's side, or another control of your own. / 21 CFR 117.130 (hazard analysis); 21 CFR 117.135(c)(5) and Subpart G (supply-chain program) / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-117/subpart-C/section-117.130 / Section 3, Hazard analysis (page 3) / inferred / Undeclared allergen if mislabeled

It does not evaluate chemical hazards for these ingredients, such as pesticide residues, mycotoxins, or natural toxins in legumes. Even if none needs a control, the evaluation has to be written down. / Add rows for chemical hazards at receiving (beans, tahini, spices), each with a written justification for whether it needs a preventive control. / 21 CFR 117.130(b)(1)(ii) / https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-117/subpart-C/section-117.130 / Section 3, Hazard analysis (page 3) / read

identity.title: Food Safety Plan (FSMA Preventive Controls for Human Food) – Ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips, Salem Plant
identity.issuer: Willamette Valley Foods, Inc. (prepared by Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager / PCQI)

scan.summary: This is your written food safety plan for the ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips made at the Salem plant, under FDA's preventive controls rule for human food (21 CFR Part 117). It is your own document, so any gaps are yours to fix. It covers most of the basics: the hazard analysis, cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal controls, monitoring, corrective actions and verification. But it has no recall plan. It also does not deal with Salmonella in tahini and the other ingredients added after the cook step, its supplier program is thinner than the rule requires, and it is not signed by the owner or operator.
scan.freshness_note: The plan took effect on 2025-05-12 and is about 16 months old. FDA requires it to be re-analysed at least every 3 years, which makes about 2028-05-12 the latest date. It must be re-analysed sooner if the products, process, suppliers or equipment change. No newer version is needed on age alone, but the gaps below call for a revision now.

gaps.title: No recall plan
gaps.description: There is a hazard requiring a preventive control, so the plan must include a written recall plan. There is none. The plan does not say how to notify customers in OR, WA and ID, how to notify the public, how to check that the recall worked, or what to do with recalled product.
gaps.fix: Add a recall plan section. Name who is responsible for each step, and set out how you will notify direct customers and the public, run effectiveness checks, and dispose of or rework recalled product. Keep your customer and distribution lists where the recall team can reach them.

gaps.title: Pathogens in ingredients added after the cook step are not assessed
gaps.description: The only hazard listed for tahini is the sesame allergen. Tahini, garlic, lemon juice, spices and olive oil are blended in after the kill step, so any Salmonella or Listeria they carry is not controlled by the cook. Tahini in particular has been linked to Salmonella outbreaks and recalls. The hazard analysis does not cover this.
gaps.fix: Add hazard analysis rows for pathogens in each ingredient added after cooking. Then name the control for each one: a supply-chain-applied control with supplier verification, a validated process step on the supplier's side, or another control of your own.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.130 (hazard analysis); 21 CFR 117.135(c)(5) and Subpart G (supply-chain program)

gaps.title: Supply-chain program lacks required elements
gaps.description: Section 8 says suppliers are approved and send a certificate and COAs. It does not describe the written supplier approval, the verification activity chosen for each hazard or how often it is done, the review of actual audit reports (a certificate alone is not enough), or written receiving procedures. For a hazard that could cause serious illness or death, such as Salmonella in tahini, the default verification is an annual onsite audit, and you review its results.
gaps.fix: Expand section 8. List which hazards the supplier controls and document the approval of each supplier. State the verification activity and frequency for each (for tahini, normally an annual onsite audit report that you review), and add written receiving procedures and the records you will keep.
gaps.quote: provide a current third-party audit certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot

gaps.title: Chemical hazards not evaluated
gaps.description: The hazard analysis lists only biological, physical and allergen hazards. It does not evaluate chemical hazards for these ingredients, such as pesticide residues, mycotoxins, or natural toxins in legumes. Even if none needs a control, the evaluation has to be written down.
gaps.fix: Add rows for chemical hazards at receiving (beans, tahini, spices), each with a written justification for whether it needs a preventive control.

gaps.title: Refrigerated storage hazard has no preventive control
gaps.description: The hazard analysis says Listeria growth in refrigerated storage needs a preventive control. Section 4 lists none for it: there is no cooler temperature limit, monitoring or corrective action. The 41°F figure appears only in the product description.
gaps.fix: Add a temperature control for cold storage (for example, product held at or below 41°F). Add continuous or periodic temperature monitoring, a corrective action for going over the limit, and the record you will keep.
gaps.quote: Refrigerated RTE product with a 45-day shelf life

gaps.title: Stones in dry beans are assigned to metal detection
gaps.description: The plan says foreign material in dry beans, including stones, is controlled at metal detection. A metal detector does not detect stones. The only other control named is supplier screening, and that is not written up as a supplier control.
gaps.fix: Name a control that actually catches stones, such as a destoner, sorting or visual inspection at receiving or soaking, or document it as a supplier-applied control with verification. Otherwise, justify in writing why stones do not need a preventive control.
gaps.quote: controlled at metal detection and by supplier screening

gaps.title: Cook critical limit may not be achievable as written
gaps.description: The cook limit is an internal temperature of at least 212°F. That is the boiling point of water at sea level. In an open kettle at Salem's elevation, product may never read 212°F, which would mean either constant deviations or records that do not reflect reality. We worked this out from physics and did not see it stated anywhere.
gaps.fix: Have the PCQI review the limit and base it on a validated time and temperature that actually kills the target pathogens. Then update sections 4, 5 and 6.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.135(c)(1) and 117.160 (unsure which a reviewer would cite)
gaps.quote: Cook beans in the kettle to an internal temperature of at least 212°F for at least 60 minutes

gaps.title: No validation of process controls
gaps.description: The cook and cooling limits are process controls. The PCQI must validate that they control the hazard, before use or within 90 days of first production. The plan cites no scientific or technical basis and no validation study.
gaps.fix: Add a validation section that cites the scientific basis for the cook and cooling parameters (literature, process authority or study) and the date the PCQI signed off. Keep the validation records.

gaps.title: Environmental monitoring and product testing procedures incomplete
gaps.description: Written procedures for environmental monitoring and product testing must name the organism, sampling locations and number of sites, timing and frequency, sampling plan, test method, the laboratory, and corrective actions. The plan gives frequencies but not the named swab sites or zones, sampling timing, sampling plan or method, or the lab.
gaps.fix: Add a written environmental monitoring and product testing procedure, or reference a separate SOP. Include a site map, sample sizes, the test method, the lab's name and accreditation, and when during production sampling is done.
gaps.quote: Finished product is tested for Listeria monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory.

gaps.title: No corrective action for a positive finished-product Listeria result
gaps.description: Section 6 covers positive environmental swabs but says nothing about what happens if the monthly finished-product test finds Listeria monocytogenes. That would mean holding the lot, evaluating it, recalling if needed, and finding the cause.
gaps.fix: Add a corrective action for a positive product result: hold or recall the affected lots, investigate the root cause, re-clean and do extra testing, and have the PCQI review. Also link finished product to the recall plan.

gaps.title: Label check at packaging not monitored
gaps.description: The allergen control says labels are reviewed at receipt and at printing. The monitoring section only records the check at receipt. Nothing checks that the right label is on the right product at filling and sealing, which is where most undeclared-allergen recalls start.
gaps.fix: Add a label check at filling or date coding (at start-up, at each product changeover and at set intervals), recorded on a log, with a corrective action for wrong labels.
gaps.quote: reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs the label log

gaps.title: Cooling monitoring does not capture the start point
gaps.description: Cooling is checked at 2 and 6 hours, but no start time or starting temperature (135°F) is recorded, so the 2-hour and 6-hour points cannot be anchored.
gaps.fix: Record the time and temperature when the product reaches 135°F, then at 2 hours and 6 hours after that.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.140 (general; unsure a reviewer would cite this specifically)
gaps.quote: The blast chiller operator records the temperature at 2 hours and at 6 hours on the cooling log.

gaps.title: Plan not signed and dated by owner, operator or agent in charge
gaps.description: The approval line shows only a job title. There is no name, signature or date, and the rule requires a signature and date when the plan is first completed and after each change.
gaps.fix: Have the owner, operator or agent in charge sign and date the plan, and add a revision history table.

gaps.title: No reanalysis commitment
gaps.description: The plan does not say it will be re-analysed at least every 3 years, or when there is a change, new hazard information, or a control that turns out not to work.
gaps.fix: Add a short reanalysis section with the triggers and the 3-year maximum.

deadlines.title: Re-analyse the food safety plan (at least every 3 years)
PCQI review of cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records
deadlines.source_line: The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven working days of their creation.

deadlines.source_line: Probe thermometers are calibrated in ice water and boiling water weekly

deadlines.title: Annual metal detector service by manufacturer
deadlines.source_line: the metal detector is serviced by the manufacturer annually

deadlines.title: Monthly finished-product Listeria monocytogenes test
deadlines.source_line: Finished product is tested for Listeria monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory.

deadlines.title: Quarterly environmental monitoring trend review
deadlines.source_line: Environmental monitoring results are trended quarterly.

deadlines.title: Annual food hygiene training for production employees
deadlines.source_line: All production employees receive food hygiene training at hire and annually.

scan.confidence_notes: All 7 pages were clear and fully read: identity and date from page 1, product and staffing from page 2, hazards on page 3, controls on page 4, monitoring and corrective actions on page 5, verification and supply chain on page 6, records and training on page 7. I am confident that there is no recall plan, no supplier verification detail, no owner signature, no refrigerated-storage control, no validation and no chemical-hazard evaluation. The points I worked out myself rather than read are these: Salmonella in tahini and other ingredients added after cooking, the 212°F internal cook limit possibly being unreachable at atmospheric pressure, stones not being caught by the metal detector, and the cooling start time. The plant's PCQI or a process authority should confirm them. Hummus is not itself on FDA's Food Traceability List (it is scored separately in FDA's risk model), so I did not raise traceability-rule records. Citations are to 21 CFR Part 117. I am less certain which exact paragraph a reviewer would cite for the cooling-start and cook-limit points, and I have said so on those items.

WILLAMETTE VALLEY FOODS, INC.
FOOD SAFETY PLAN
Ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips
Salem Plant, 1850 Fairgrounds Road NE, Salem, Oregon 97301
Effective date: May 12, 2025
Prepared by: Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager, Preventive Controls Qualified Individual
(PCQI certificate, FSPCA course, March 2024)
Approved by: Plant Manager
1. Facility and product description
Willamette Valley Foods produces refrigerated ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips in 8-ounce and 16-
ounce sealed plastic tubs for retail sale in Oregon, Washington and Idaho. The Salem plant operates one
shift, five days a week, with 28 production employees. Products are made from cooked chickpeas or black
beans, tahini, lemon juice, garlic, olive oil, salt and spices, blended, filled, sealed, coded and held
refrigerated at or below 41°F. Shelf life is 45 days refrigerated. Products are labeled with the allergen
statement "Contains: sesame" for all hummus items.
2. Process flow
Receiving of dry beans, tahini and other ingredients → dry storage or refrigerated storage → soaking and
cooking of beans (kettle, 212°F, 60 minutes minimum) → cooling in the blast chiller → blending with
other ingredients → filling and sealing → date coding → metal detection → refrigerated storage →
shipping.

4. Preventive controls

growth at cooling and to 41°F within a further 4 hours in the blast chiller 4 hours
Listeria in the Sanitation of food-contact surfaces before each Sanitation ATP swab pass before start-up; Listeria
RTE environment production run and between products; environmental spp. swabs, 10 sites weekly, zone 1 and 2
monitoring swabs weekly
Sesame allergen Allergen labeling review for every label at receipt and at Allergen Label matches the formulation sheet;
printing; product scheduling with hummus items last in washdown verified by ATP swab before
the day, followed by full washdown the next non-sesame product
Metal Metal detection of every sealed tub Process Reject at 2.0 mm ferrous, 2.5 mm non-
ferrous, 3.0 mm stainless test pieces
5. Monitoring
The kettle operator records the internal temperature and the time at the start and end of each cook batch
on the cook log. The blast chiller operator records the temperature at 2 hours and at 6 hours on the cooling
log. The sanitation lead records the ATP swab result before each start-up. The line lead runs the three
metal test pieces through the detector at start-up, every two hours, and at the end of the run, and records
the result. The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs
the label log.
6. Corrective actions
If a cook batch does not reach 212°F for 60 minutes, the batch is re-cooked to the critical limit or
discarded, and the cause is recorded. If cooling exceeds the time limits, the batch is discarded. If an ATP
swab fails, the surface is re-cleaned and re-swabbed before production starts. If a Listeria spp. swab is
positive, the site is cleaned and re-swabbed, adjacent sites are added, and product made on that line since
the last negative swab is held pending investigation. If the metal detector fails a test piece, all product
since the last passing test is re-run through the detector. If a label does not match the formulation, the lot
is quarantined and not used. All corrective actions are recorded on the corrective action log and reviewed
by the PCQI within seven days.
7. Verification
The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven
working days of their creation. Probe thermometers are calibrated in ice water and boiling water weekly,
and the metal detector is serviced by the manufacturer annually. Finished product is tested for Listeria
monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory. Environmental monitoring results are trended
quarterly.
8. Supply-chain program
Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit
certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot. The approved supplier list is maintained by the quality
manager.
9. Records
All records named in this plan are kept at the Salem plant for at least two years from the date of the record
and are available to FDA and the Oregon Department of Agriculture on request. Records are reviewed and
signed by the PCQI as described in section 7.
10. Training
All production employees receive food hygiene training at hire and annually. The PCQI holds a current
FSPCA certificate. Sanitation and line leads are trained on the monitoring procedures in this plan.
